items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. Dollar General, which operates more than 21,000 stores, overcharged by millions of dollars in violation of federal and state consumer protection laws, according to a lawsuit filed in Tennessee federal court. The pricing discrepancies from 2019 through March 2026 led to almost 30,000 consumer complaints to the company, demonstrating “pervasive and systemic pricing inaccuracies,” federal and state enforcers said. “Rather than ensuring its prices at checkout are accurate, for years Dollar General avoided implementing safeguards to prevent continued overcharging, effectively shifting the burden of its own operational shortcomings onto the very communities and consumers who can least afford it,” the complaint alleged. Dollar General didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Between 2019 and 2026, the company entered into seven settlements in six different states related to inaccurate pricing, paying a total of $6 million in penalties, the complaint said. This event will highlight AI-powered tools that identify suspicious activity, prevent leakage, and support regulatory compliance across underwriting and claims. Vendors will highlight pattern recognition, claims fraud detection, premium fraud detection, compliance monitoring and audit automation. In partnership with Insurance Journal, Risky Future’s AI Tools for Fraud Detection and Compliance Demo Day will be held on Wednesday, October 28, beginning at 1pm ET. Visit the event’s website to register for this free event. Each sponsored presentation, demo or case study will run between 15 and 20 minutes. Speakers include representatives from the following companies: CCC Intelligent Solutions: CCC Fraud Solutions help auto insurers proactively identify potential fraud in near-real time with intelligence connected across claims, photos, and carriers. Designed for Special Investigation Units (SIUs), the portfolio brings photo intelligence, cross-carrier data, and intelligent intervention rules into the claims workflow. These capabilities help SIU teams surface risk indicators, prioritize referrals, and gain additional context to guide investigations, inform next steps, and support a more proactive approach to fraud detection. Truepic: Truepic Vision helps businesses trust what they see — authenticating visuals, blocking AI manipulation, and providing insights to prevent fraud. Wisedocs: Wisedocs is the decision intelligence platform for insurance claims. The company helps insurers and organizations across the claims ecosystem transform complex claim documents into structured, decision-ready intelligence. Using artificial intelligence combined with expert human oversight, Wisedocs organizes, analyzes, and summarizes large volumes of medical, legal, and billing records so claims teams can identify risk earlier, make faster decisions, and improve claim outcomes. It is a product of Insurance Journal, the property/casualty insurance industry’s leading daily news website, providing research, breaking news, online media products and much more. items.extracted_text: Sidecars and data centres key opportunity areas for HCMA in 2027: CEO Madea - Artemis.bm Sidecars and data centres key opportunity areas for HCMA in 2027: CEO Madea - Artemis.bm Sidecars and data centres key opportunity areas for HCMA in 2027: CEO Madea 26th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As the collateralized reinsurance sidecar market continues to expand, and momentum builds around the data centre build-out, Jarad Madea, Chief Executive Officer of Howden Capital Markets & Advisory (HCMA) told Artemis that those are key areas where HCMA sees future opportunities as the industry begins to head into 2027. Speaking to Artemis during the reinsurance conference season, Madea discussed how HCMA plans to work more directly with institutional investors looking to deploy capital into casualty sidecars, as well as what he believes are the most exciting opportunities for investors in the reinsurance market today. In regard to reinsurance, Madea says there is a breadth of opportunity in the market, and says “it is a very interesting time in reinsurance and insurance, particularly for end-investors who maybe haven’t participated in the space as much.” “Just as one anecdote, three to five years ago, there were two investors and true end-investors here in Monte Carlo. This year, I think there are probably 20 true end-investors at least, and I’m sure there are others that I haven’t seen or spoken to,” Madea said. To illustrate, Madea mentioned that a recent HCMA capital markets dinner brought together about 15 investors and 15 clients to help match capital directly with risk. “The point is that there is a lot of interest in the space from end-investors who are looking for creative ways to invest in insurance,” Madea said. “The most exciting part is the interest level and the amount of money that is out there globally, and the interest in participating directly in the risk of the insurance space. It’s also about being able to innovate around different structures and deals that can match what they’re looking for with what our clients are looking for in different ways” the CEO continued. “That’s what’s exciting. And then, on the risk side, it’s about what’s of interest to those investors. It continues to be about finding incremental areas to generate risk-adjusted returns and the diversification that our industry brings to those investors, outside of their other core investment themes.” Madea also underscored how there has been an influx of attractive returns recorded over the last several years, both on the balance sheet for insurers, reinsurers and for investors, whether that being catastrophe bond investors, property sidecar investors, or whole-account casualty sidecar-type transactions. “Those returns are structured to be very attractive. Obviously, it will take time to see how they play out, but I think the most exciting thing is the creativity that the space is offering to allow those investors to structure and generate the risk-adjusted returns that they need across the spectrum,” Madea said. Turning back to sidecars, Madea emphasised that expanding these structures across different platforms and geographies will be a central focus for HCMA in 2027. “Casualty sidecars or whole-account casualty sidecars, and that could be through Lloyd’s, through fronting companies, Bermuda balance sheets, or US primary balance sheets. So, broadening that with different types of structures, and then also geographies, whether it’s US risk, global risk or European risk, I think that’s going to be a big focus of ours,” Madea explained. “The other focus on that is not only helping our clients with it, but also on helping and advising investors. Last year, there was one of these transactions where we advised the investor side, similar to our M&A advisory, in which we’re either advising a buyer or a seller, and often advising on both sides in different deals,” the CEO continued. “Similarly, we’d like to be able to help investors evaluate these transactions as an advisor on their side as well, in deals that are for clients we’re not already involved with. We don’t have every single client, obviously, but we can advise investors in those transactions. There’s a lot for us to do in that space in many different roles.” Data centres are another major area of focus HCMA heading into 2027, as well as finding ways to expand alternative capital more across Europe and outside the United States, according to Madea “Regarding data centres. I would love for us to be able to find and work on solutions to bring capacity there as well. And then, just globally, how do we continue to expand this alternative capital more in Europe and outside of the US and into broader areas as well? I think that’s going to be an opportunity and a focus for us. In recent months, there has been a lot of noise across the industry regarding the rapid data centre build-out. However, few conversations appear to focus on how ILS investors can tap into this growth. This gap leads Madea to believe that the sector offers a strong opportunity for the ILS industry, though he notes that no finalised solutions exist yet. While acknowledging the risks involved, the CEO stresses that the insurance market can play a crucial role in guiding development and hopes the industry finds ways for alternative capital to participate too. “I hope we can find ways for alternative capital to participate. Obviously, there’s a tremendous amount of money there to help solve this issue. I don’t think there’s going to be anything that gets solved without traditional insurers and reinsurers, though. I don’t think there’s anybody that’s going to solve it on their own, with just capital. You need to do it in conjunction with traditional insurers and reinsurers as part of the ecosystem,” Madea explained. He continued: “Then it’s about managing and solving for some of the aggregation risk. How do you do that? It’s a way to broaden the portfolio geographically, a way to broaden the risk. More importantly, maybe there are incremental risks that come out of data centres and AI that can broaden the portfolio of risks and make it a little more diversified.” “How do you structure that aggregation risk, particularly in those concentrations, so it’s not so capital-heavy in terms of what needs to be collateralised from the ILS market? That will be difficult to do and still get the returns that would be needed to support that capital, while having the ultimate customer pay something appropriate,” Madea concluded. items.extracted_text: Insurers lean on third-party capital, strategic partnerships to manage operating models: BlackRock - Artemis.bm Insurers lean on third-party capital, strategic partnerships to manage operating models: BlackRock - Artemis.bm Insurers lean on third-party capital, strategic partnerships to manage operating models: BlackRock 27th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard BlackRock’s 15th annual survey of the global insurance industry found that insurance capital solutions have become a critical part of how insurers manage their businesses, highlighting that third-party capital partnerships can help allocate risk and capital more effectively, while preserving the capacity to compete, invest in growth, and meet policyholder obligations. BlackRock’s survey, which includes perspectives of 463 insurers across 31 markets representing investable assets of more than $24 trillion, underscored how central partnerships are becoming to insurers’ operating models. The role of these partnerships extends beyond investment management with 82% of insurers reporting external partnerships across at least two business functions, spanning investments, capital provision, liability and product design, and distribution. Mark Erickson, Global Insurance Strategist in BlackRock’s Financial Institutions Group, commented: “Insurers are increasingly looking for partners that can do more than manage investments. To achieve their long-term objectives, insurers are looking across investment, capital, and technology holistically to navigate an increasingly complex operating environment. Bringing these capabilities together is the defining competitive advantage in this market.” In addition, BlackRock’s report acknowledges that the sources of capital and capabilities available to the insurance industry continue to broaden. “Traditional insurers and reinsurers are increasingly complemented by, and competing with, institutional and private capital, while asset managers are bringing investment origination, portfolio construction, and risk-management capabilities into insurance partnerships in an aligned manner. The result is a more interconnected ecosystem spanning underwriting, risk transfer, capital allocation, and asset management,” the report reads. “For property and casualty and specialty insurers, sidecars and third-party capital can provide stable underwriting capacity and help manage concentrations and peak-loss exposures. For life and annuity insurers, funded and asset-intensive reinsurance can support capital management, risk transfer, and new-business growth. Across sectors and jurisdictions, these options often involve one or more strategic investment partners who can provide access to asset classes, origination capabilities, and operating infrastructure that may be difficult or inefficient to build internally.” Moreover, BlackRock’s report also underlines how capital management is becoming more deliberate and integrated across insurers’ balance sheets. “Insurers’ capital-management intentions point to selective expansion in the use of tools. Captive onshore reinsurance stands out, with 53% planning to increase its use, while most expect to maintain their use of debt issuance (58%) and equity issuance (56%). Insurers’ use of capital-management tools is primarily motivated by three objectives: enhancing capital efficiency (66%) addressing regulatory, rating agency, and solvency constraints (59%) and reducing earnings volatility (50%). Achieving these outcomes, however, is often constrained by a range of challenges. Regulatory, solvency, and rating-agency constraints are the most frequently cited barrier (60%), followed by limited availability or high cost of third-party capital (43%), and operational readiness (41%),” BlackRock added. Robin M. Raju CFO, Equitable, said: “Insurers have more ways than ever to create and release capital, including reinsurance, sidecars, and alternative capital structures. The value of these tools, however, depends on how they are used. Effective capital management requires deliberate choices about which risks to retain, where capital is most productive, and how much capacity to preserve through the cycle. As these options expand, deploying capital well is becoming as important as generating it.” BlackRock also noted that as insurers, reinsurers, asset managers, and capital providers become more interconnected, capital solutions are likely to become more integrated and diverse. However, while this shift creates greater scope to combine underwriting, investments, and risk transfer, BlackRock cautions that this will also raise expectations around governance, transparency, and counterparty management. Given this, the report underscores that partner selection should demonstrate the same disciplines that are employed in structuring transactions, while simultaneously ensuring that the partnership possesses the capacity to withstand adverse circumstances when market conditions diverge from the underlying assumptions that informed the establishment of the arrangement. The firm also underscored that this competitive advantage will ultimately come from insurers deciding which risks to retain or transfer, as well as which capabilities to build internally, and which to access through partnerships. “Ultimately, capital solutions should be judged by whether they make the insurer stronger: more resilient through stress, more flexible in deploying capital, and better positioned to pursue growth while delivering on policyholder commitments. Access to capital matters, but lasting value comes from combining the right capital, capabilities, and partnerships in a way that works across cycles,” BlackRock added. BlackRock’s survey also underlined how insurers are increasingly seeking more partnerships to ramp up their capital-related activities, with 57% of respondents saying that they engage in partnerships that way. items.title: Anthropic Filing Reveals Concerns Over Data Center Pushback
items.original_title: Anthropic Filing Reveals Concerns Over Data Center Pushback
items.rss_title: Anthropic Filing Reveals Concerns Over Data Center Pushback
items.rss_description: Anthropic PBC says it expects to face heightened scrutiny of how it tackles environmental and social tensions associated with the build-out of AI infrastructure. The company, which publicly filed for an initial public offering on Monday, said it’s aware its …
items.extracted_text: Anthropic Filing Reveals Concerns Over Data Center Pushback Article 0 Comments Anthropic PBC says it expects to face heightened scrutiny of how it tackles environmental and social tensions associated with the build-out of AI infrastructure. The company, which publicly filed for an initial public offering on Monday, said it’s aware its efforts to secure power may face regulatory hurdles if there’s a perception its activities are impacting utility costs or the environment more broadly. “Data center development has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use,” the company noted in its IPO filing. At the same time, Anthropic’s “brand is subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts,” it also said. The companies building out the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence have faced increasing pushback from local communities worried about the impact on precious resources. Last month, it emerged that Oracle Corp. had cited force majeure after opposition from environmental nonprofits and regulatory setbacks complicated efforts to secure power for a data center campus in New Mexico. That project is intended to provide computing power for OpenAI. Across the US, at least 106 data center projects — representing about $198 billion in investments — were blocked or delayed amid local opposition during the first half of this year, according to Data Center Watch, a monitor run by AI intelligence firm 10a Labs. A September poll by University of Massachusetts Amherst puts US voter opposition to local AI data centers at 65%, compared with just 11% in favor. Anthropic noted in its filing that environmental standards applicable to power generation “continue to evolve, including as a result of changing governmental priorities and shifting public and political views regarding climate change and the appropriate treatment of various power generation sources.” It added that any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, as well as any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity — or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs — could “adversely affect our cost structure.” Such hurdles would have the potential to “limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.” Anthropic also highlighted climate change and environmental concerns more broadly as risk factors, including the potential fallout of extreme weather. “The physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time, as higher average temperatures can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend,” it said. Such concerns “are now core financial and fiduciary considerations, not side issues,” said Blaine Townsend, director of sustainable, responsible & impact investing at Bailard, a wealth and asset management firm. How global warming impacts businesses poses a growing risk for investors as increasingly destructive storms, droughts and floods threaten infrastructure. The seriousness with which a company treats such threats is therefore something some shareholders are monitoring more closely. Lionella Pezza, director of impact research at Domini Impact Investments, said Anthropic’s IPO filing is a reflection of just how important sustainability is for AI companies. At the same time, “there is not sufficient disclosure about the company’s environmental impact,” and the filing “contains no quantitative information on Anthropic’s greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, or water use,” she said. The risks identified are discussed only “in general terms,” Pezza added. “What is missing is any assessment of where that exposure sits, how large it is, and what it could mean for costs, computing capacity, and service continuity. Adequate disclosure should address both the company’s impact on the environment and the risks that environmental constraints pose to its business.” The Anthropic filing contrasts with SpaceX’s, which had no mention of climate change. SpaceX subsequently amended its filing to add water scarcity as a risk factor. Artificial intelligence companies have come under scrutiny from activist groups, community members, regulators and investors. Some states have pushed for moratoriums on new data center builds as they assess the potential impact to the environment and power prices. Anthropic acknowledged in its S-1 that this backlash could result in reputational harm to its business. “What we’d want to see, industrywide, is disclosure standards that keep pace with that reality, not just risk factors written to protect against liability, but a real accounting of environmental and social externalities,” Townsend said. Bailard’s research has highlighted three specific categories in which AI’s environmental footprint is material: data centers disproportionately located in communities already burdened by pollution, AI’s water use and its energy demand, Townsend said. “When we evaluate an AI company’s disclosures, we look for whether they address each of these three categories specifically.” Anthropic also referred to “increasing scrutiny” related to its ESG practices and reporting “both in the United States and internationally.” And it mentioned a “particular focus on concerns relating to AI and its impact on society and the environment,” including the power-intensive nature of its business, public concern about water usage and the reliance on critical minerals. “Some investors may use these non-financial performance factors to guide their investment strategies and, in some cases, may choose not to invest in us if they believe our policies and actions relating to ESG are inadequate,” it said. items.extracted_text: Court Rejects Exxon Appeal of $815M Award to Mechanic Over Benzene Exposure Article 0 Comments Exxon Mobil Corp. has lost its appeal of an $815.5 million compensatory damages judgment that was awarded to a Mobil gas station mechanic who developed leukemia after years of exposure to benzene in its gasoline. On October 15, a three-judge panel of the Superior Court of Pennsylvania upheld the award, ruling in part that the oil giant’s challenges to the causation evidence and other issues in its appeal should have been but were not raised at trial. The Superior Court panel also rejected Exxon’s claims that the award should be invalidated because it was “shockingly excessive and against the weight of the evidence.” Plaintiff Paul Gill was exposed to benzene while working as a mechanic and gas attendant at an ExxonMobil service station in Potter County from 1974 to 1979. As part of his work, Gill used ExxonMobil gasoline to clean automobile parts, which was a common practice at the time. He did not wear gloves or other protective equipment because he did not know that he could be exposed to benzene in gasoline through inhalation and skin contact. Gill was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia years later in 2019. He maintained that his exposure to Exxon’s gasoline some 40 years ago was a substantial factor contributing to the cause of his cancer and the leukemia has taken a “drastic toll” on his standard of living and his marriage. His complaint described a host of medical effects: He underwent blood transfusions and a stem-cell transplant suffered loss of eye, liver, and skin function as well as chronic weakness, severe pain, depression and the stiffening of his joints and suffered from seizures and has gone into diabetic coma. Also, the cancer spread to his colon, liver and lungs. He has had to isolate himself from friends and family for fear that he will contract diseases from them. Product Liability Gill brought counts of negligence and product-defect strict liability against Exxon. In the May 2024 trial in the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas jurors heard evidence that ExxonMobil was aware decades ago that there is no safe level of benzene exposure and that Exxon failed to warn Gill of this dangerous and potentially lethal defect in its product, even though “the American Petroleum Institute advised its members, including ExxonMobil, that there was no safe level of benzene exposure in 1948.” Exxon’s defense argued in part that Gill and his medical experts failed to prove that the gasoline caused his cancer. The oil giant maintained that instead of focusing on the gasoline product for which Exxon was sued, the plaintiff’s witnesses focused on benzene which is a separate and distinct product. The jury sided with Gill. Jurists found that Exxon was negligent, that its gasoline was defectively designed, and that it had failed to warn about the known dangers of exposure to benzene in its gasoline. The jury awarded Gill a total of $725,000,000 for the pain and suffering, embarrassment and humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, and disfigurement that the leukemia caused him. The jury also awarded his wife $500,000 for loss of consortium. The verdict was later increased by roughly $90 million in delay damages, bringing the judgment to almost $816 million Exxon moved for post-trial relief and sought a judgment notwithstanding the verdict (JNOV), a new trial, or remittitur of the jury verdict. The lower court denied Exxon’s post-trial requests. The firm then filed an appeal challenging the trial court’s rulings on a number of fronts in the Superior Court. However, the appeals court denied the oil company’s challenges to evidence on causation because they had not been raised at trial and also denied its arguments on alleged juror misconduct. The court upheld the trial court in its decisions related to causation testimony from medical experts and its decisions not to order a new trial or reduce the jury’s $725 million compensatory damages award. The Superior Court declined to impose its judgment of a fair and reasonable award over that of the trial court. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Guidewire to Buy UK Insurance AI Firm hyperexponential in Deal Worth Up to $2.1B Article 0 Comments Insurance software maker Guidewire said on Tuesday it would buy hyperexponential for $1.7 billion in cash and up to $400 million more if revenue targets are met, to expand into AI tools that help insurers assess price and risk. London-based hyperexponential makes AI-powered underwriting and pricing software for commercial property and casualty insurers. The deal will let AI agents work alongside underwriters to assess risk, price it and make decisions, Guidewire said. It will fund the deal with $1 billion in new term loans from Bank of America and Citibank as well as cash on hand. The deal is expected to close in the second quarter of Guidewire’s fiscal 2027 and will not affect its first-quarter forecast. Guidewire’s whose software is used by more than 570 property and casualty insurers in 44 countries. (Reporting by Anzar Mehraj in Bengaluru editing by Joyjeet Das) Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.extracted_text: Novo Nordisk Loses Court Ruling Over Eli Lilly Obesity Drug Ads Article 0 Comments Novo Nordisk A/S lost a bid in a U.S. court to temporarily block Eli Lilly & Co. U.S. District Judge Zahid Quraishi ruled Monday that Lilly can continue to make the disputed claims in its ads while Novo proceeds with a lawsuit it filed in July in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey. The judge said that Novo’s case for a preliminary injunction was “less than persuasive” because it failed to show irreparable harm. The dispute involves two sets of ads by Lilly. In one, the drugmaker claims its Zepbound obesity drug is superior to Novo’s Wegovy weight-loss medication. In the other, Lilly says its Mounjaro controls type 2 diabetes better than Novo’s Ozempic. The suit claims the comparisons amount to false advertising because Lilly relied on research that didn’t examine higher doses of Novo’s drugs that are more effective than its lower doses. Both drugmakers seek to boost their share of a global market for obesity treatments that Bloomberg Intelligence estimates could reach $120 billion a year by 2030. Novo once dominated the market with Wegovy, but Lilly caught up with Zepbound and now has the lead in sales. Lilly said in a statement that it was pleased with the ruling. “Our focus has been and continues to be on the millions of people living with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic diseases,” the Indianapolis-based company said. Novo didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: Chiquita Sees Cheap Bananas at Risk on El Niño Supply Threat
items.original_title: Chiquita Sees Cheap Bananas at Risk on El Niño Supply Threat
items.rss_title: Chiquita Sees Cheap Bananas at Risk on El Niño Supply Threat
items.rss_description: Bananas are in danger of becoming the next item in the grocery aisles to see price hikes, thanks in part to a powerful El Niño and war, says one of the top sellers of the fruit. “The industry is facing …
items.extracted_text: Chiquita Sees Cheap Bananas at Risk on El Niño Supply Threat Article 0 Comments Bananas are in danger of becoming the next item in the grocery aisles to see price hikes, thanks in part to a powerful El Niño and war, says one of the top sellers of the fruit. “The industry is facing extreme weather conditions, facing geopolitical disruptions,” Carlos López Flores, chief executive officer of Chiquita Brands International, said in an interview. “The economics to produce tropical fruit is getting more expensive.” Related: Money Managers Say There’s Nowhere to Hide as Super El Niño Forms The CEO predicts the industry will sell fewer bananas in 2027 and likely at a higher cost, potentially making next year the most difficult for the industry in decades. “We are forecasting a very challenging end of 2026 and a very challenging start of next year for the industry,” he said, adding that El Niño and geopolitical disruptions make it more difficult for Latin America suppliers to grow bananas. That could ultimately mean higher prices for consumers who’ve been shielded from price hikes for years. Food prices around the world have soared, thanks to elevated costs to grow and transport agricultural goods along with war-related disruptions and the impacts of bad weather on crops. Bananas largely avoided price volatility, providing stability to consumers trying to tame rising household grocery bills. Bananas generated $12.8 billion in export revenue in 2025, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. But companies have faced slim margins for years, having to source supply year-round and race the fruit across the world before it ripens, all to sell for less than a dollar a pound. Chiquita is one of the world’s biggest banana traders, whose iconic brand dates back more than 80 years, so the CEO’s outlook carries weight. The company has its own farms and also buys from outside suppliers, sourcing all its fruit from Latin America. López Flores said the Middle East conflict has already pushed up costs for fuel, fertilizer and packaging that have been hard to pass on to customers. Now, he sees an intensifying El Niño posing a new threat for Latin America, the world’s top banana exporting region. The phenomenon brings heavy rains across Ecuador and Peru while triggering severe droughts across the Amazon basin and northeastern Brazil. Flooding downpours in Ecuador, the top supplier, can amplify plant disease, spoil crops and wash out roads. El Niño-driven drought can sap Panama Canal water levels, undercutting a vital shipping link for nearby growing nations. Chiquita is already in early negotiations with retailers about supply deals and pricing for next year, López Flores said. Talks so far have been more about “surety of supply” than price hikes, but he said Chiquita has discussed with buyers the added costs filtering through the banana supply chain. The industry typically sells most bananas through long-term deals on future output at fixed costs, giving suppliers little ability to pass on unexpected increases in farm costs. It’s unclear how willing retailers would be willing to accept higher prices or how those would sit with consumers, who are used to bananas being among the cheapest items at the grocery store. Bananas sold in US cities averaged around 66 cents a pound last month, according to government data, less than half the price of oranges and grapefruit. Unlike other pantry staples, banana prices have barely budged for years — rising just 14% over a decade. López Flores said Chiquita is committed to providing a reliable source of bananas to customers and consumers despite the struggles of Latin American producers. “Everybody in that region who grows bananas will tell you today it is more difficult, more expensive and less predictable to grow bananas than it was a year ago,” he said. “It will be more challenging.” Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: John Seo on 25 years in the catastrophe bond business: Artemis Live video interview - Artemis.bm John Seo on 25 years in the catastrophe bond business: Artemis Live video interview - Artemis.bm John Seo on 25 years in the catastrophe bond business: Artemis Live video interview 27th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans With specialist catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager Fermat Capital Management celebrating its 25th birthday this year, for our latest Artemis Live video interview we spoke with co-founder and Managing Director of the firm John Seo . The company manages more than $11 billion of investments across catastrophe bonds and related insurance-linked securities and J ohn Seo gave us an insight into how he views the market’s development over the 25 year history of Fermat Capital Management and his expectations for the future of the ILS industry . We discussed Fermat Capital Management’s 25-year history in the catastrophe bond and ILS business, as well as opportunities and challenges for the asset class’ future. Seo talked us through how he undertook the task of selecting a list of 25 notable catastrophe bond transactions from across Fermat’s history, saying they were chosen as a representative, partly subjective selection from deals where Fermat had been a lead investor. He also explained some of the lessons he’s learned through his long-tenure in the ILS industry , noting the importance as an investment manager of compounding knowledge over-time to improve returns while managing risk. We discussed how market cycles have changed and whether traditional insurance, reinsurance and ILS market cycles are coming more into phase in 2026. On the future of the industry, Seo identified on-shoring of cat bond and ILS structures as a way to catalyse more rapid adoption and market expansion, while also commenting on the data centre risk transfer opportunity. Seo said that a larger ILS market could support more orderly issuance and result in substantial market growth , enabling the catastrophe bond and capital market investors to support a greater proportion of the world’s natural disaster risks, as well as other catastrophic exposures. Watch the full video interview to learn much more about Fermat Capital Management’s 25 year journey in the catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities market.
